## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trial results yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so any non-zero score tells us something. With the default recipe the budget allows only 32 PPO updates (131k steps), which is probably too few for exact multi-brick builds. Two levers look most promising: more and smaller updates, and a longer reward horizon so the +1 exact-build bonus counts for more. The architecture also has a structural weakness. Its head only pools features over the brick footprint. The task needs a two-stage judgement: first find the landing layer (the maximum height under the footprint), then check each covered cell's target at that layer. A head that sends the pooled footprint value back to every covered cell and pools again can learn that check. The three trials separate the two levers: A is recipe only, B adds the new head (A vs B), and C changes the PPO epochs (B vs C).

### Round 2
Every trial scored 0, both on dev and on training success in the last 10% of training. That holds for the baseline recipe with 2 epochs, the gather head and the 1-epoch run. Since nothing ever succeeded, we cannot tell whether the recipe or the head was the limit. The networks most likely get the core geometry wrong. A brick lands at the highest point under its footprint, and it is right only if the target's layer at that height matches the footprint and the cells below are already filled. The 2D trunks fold all layers into column features, so they have to work out which layer a brick lands on, and compare it with the target at that layer, from pooled 'height-like' features alone. Two designs might fix this. A layer-resolved head handles each layer z separately, sees layers z-1 and z+1, pools over footprints, and attends across layers to pick the landing layer. A footprint-kernel head instead gives a deeper trunk direct per-cell convolutions over each footprint. With every score at zero, any nonzero 2-seed result is a real signal.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on both seeds, including training success in the last 10% of training. That was true across three head designs (footprint pooling, gather-repool, layer-resolved), a deeper trunk, and recipes with 1–2 epochs, gamma up to 0.99 and up to about 370k steps. Since nothing got off zero, no change so far has had a measurable effect. One thing every design shared is a head that pools over the footprint from the top-left anchor. If this world uses a different anchor or footprint orientation (the task warns the world may differ from its description), every head so far computed features over the wrong cells. This round tests heads that don't assume a convention: a learned 3x3 output kernel lets each brick type work out its own footprint offsets. Candidate 2 changes only the recipe of candidate 1, toward maximum sample count. Candidate 3 adds global self-attention.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0 on every seed, and training success also stayed at 0. That held across every head type (footprint pooling, gather, per-layer, footprint-kernel, 3x3 conv, attention), across depths, and across recipes (1–2 epochs, 140k–400k steps, gamma 0.95–0.99). When nothing learns even on training designs, the cause is probably something every design shares, not capacity. The task warns that the world may not behave as described. Every head so far assumes that action index t*Y*X + y*X + x is the logit at feature cell (y, x). If the world transposes, flips or interleaves this order (cell-major instead of type-major), no spatially equivariant head can learn it. The 3x3 head only covers small shifts. This round tests heads that work under any convention: one sums logit maps over all orientations and both index orders, one adds a fully connected head that can learn any mapping, and one combines both.
